name: Vacuum Tubes
jpcub_source: Device physics: tube power ≈1W/gate; ENIAC ~150kW for ~5k adds/sec → O(10^[-2,-1]) J/op
efficiency_trend: Flat during tube era; improvement from device miniaturization (miniature tubes) marginal
paradigm_switch_driver: Reliability (tube burnout), not energy — transistor transition driven by reliability and size
risk_flag: R-01: archival data for 1940s-50s computing limited to equipment manuals and oral histories

name: Discrete Transistors
jpcub_source: IBM System/360 specs; transistor switching energy O(10^(-9)) J/gate; macro-level ~10^(3-4) gates/op
jpcub_anchor: IBM System/360 Model 91 specifications; published transistor switching energy
efficiency_trend: JPCUB improved ~3 orders of magnitude from vacuum tubes; still dominated by device physics, not architecture
paradigm_switch_driver: Reliability + size + power; transistor enabled compact, reliable logic but energy was secondary driver

name: CMOS VLSI (Microprocessor)
representative_system: Intel 4004 (1971) → Intel 8086 (1978) → Intel Pentium (1993) → Intel Pentium 4 (2000)
jpcub_source: CMOS gate switching C*V^2; Intel processor datasheets (4004→Pentium 4); Dennard scaling data
jpcub_anchor: Intel microprocessor datasheets (1971-2000); Dennard (1974) scaling paper
efficiency_trend: Exponential improvement via Dennard scaling (~2×/18mo); JPCUB tracks transistor count — leading indicator of MOS process node transitions
paradigm_switch_driver: CMOS replaced NMOS/bipolar due to power; Dennard scaling broke around 2005, forcing multi-core transition

name: Multi-core Parallelism
representative_system: Intel Core 2 Duo (2006) → Intel Xeon E5 (2012)
jpcub_source: SPEC Power dataset (Tröpgen 2024, C4); Intel Ark datasheets; Koomey's law data
jpcub_anchor: Tröpgen et al. (2024) SPEC Power 16-yr data, arXiv:2411.07062
efficiency_trend: JPCUB improvement slowed significantly post-Dennard; multi-core improved throughput but NOT per-op energy cost; the 'dark silicon' era
paradigm_switch_driver: Dennard scaling breakdown forced parallelization; energy per op stopped improving at historical rate — JPCUB signal FLATTENS as transition driver

name: GPU / SIMD Acceleration
jpcub_source: NVIDIA GPU specifications (K20→V100→A100); SPEC Power (C4); Koomey's law extension data
jpcub_anchor: NVIDIA GPU whitepapers; Tröpgen et al. (2024) SPEC Power
efficiency_trend: GPU transition was efficiency-driven; JPCUB was a LEADING indicator — GPUs won on FLOPS/Watt before winning on absolute FLOPS
paradigm_switch_driver: Energy efficiency was Central driver — GPU parallelism exploited workload-level parallelism to reduce J/op; JPCUB LED the transition

name: AI Accelerators (TPU/NPU)
representative_system: Google TPU v1 (2016) → NVIDIA H100 (2022) → custom NPUs (2024)
jpcub_source: Google TPU ISCA paper (Jouppi 2017, C5 benchmark analog); NVIDIA H100 whitepaper; TokenPowerBench (C5/Niu); xPU-athalon (C6/Golden)
jpcub_anchor: Jouppi et al. (2017) TPU ISCA; Niu et al. (2025) TokenPowerBench, arXiv:2512.03024; Golden et al. (2026) xPU-athalon, arXiv:2604.10852
efficiency_trend: JPCUB is THE driver — domain-specific architectures win on J/op; absolute performance is derivative of efficiency improvement; JPCUB strongly LEADING
paradigm_switch_driver: Energy-per-inference is THE gating metric for AI deployment; JPCUB leading indicator confirmed — TPU→NPU transition anticipated by J/op trajectory
